name: pdfcrack
why: Brute-force PDF password recovery exposes how the encryption schemes work, though the tool itself is fairly familiar to security folks.

brief.what_it_is: pdfcrack is a command-line password recovery tool for PDF files, written in C and licensed under the GPL. Per its homepage, it is a GNU/Linux tool that should also work on other POSIX-compatible systems, and it has no external dependencies. It takes an encrypted PDF and tries candidate passwords against it, either from a wordlist or by brute force, and reports the password it recovers. The homepage also says it can recover content from PDFs. The homepage lists both user passwords and owner passwords as targets.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes it simply as 'a Password Recovery Tool for PDF-files' and 'small, command line driven without external dependencies'. It is aimed at recovering access to PDFs whose passwords have been forgotten.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage says it supports the standard security handler (revision 2, 3 and 4) on all known PDF versions. It accepts either a wordlist or brute-force search, and applies simple permutations, currently only trying the first character as uppercase. It can save and load a running job, and includes a simple benchmark mode. When the user password is already known, it has an optimised search for the owner password.
brief.install_notes: Nothing beyond the Homebrew formula was visible. The formula provides a pdfcrack executable. The homepage and SourceForge page describe no accounts, runtimes or configuration. Their download pages were not fetched, so build steps are unknown.
brief.standout: It is small and has no external dependencies, and its feature list reaches past plain user-password recovery to owner-password cracking, with an optimised owner search when the user password is known. Save/load of a running job is also useful for long brute-force runs. The scout note frames it as a window into how the PDF encryption schemes work, which is plausible but not something the homepage itself says.
brief.status: Quiet to maintained at best. The homepage footer reads 'Last modified: 2008, 08 Jul, Tue'. The SourceForge project page, fetched as a second source, shows Status: Beta, a 'Last Update' of 2025-09-14, a 'Registered' date of 2006-05-26, and 497 downloads this week. That last-update date may reflect a file upload rather than a code commit, and no release notes or commit history were checked.
brief.caveats: A SourceForge user review from 2018 says it uses only one core and does not multi-thread. A 2015 review says the same. The homepage is dated 2008 and the project is marked Beta. No commands appeared in the fetched text, so usage syntax was not confirmed from source. The SourceForge page is noisy, and the review text came from it rather than from the author. The Homebrew formula has an empty caveats field.
quotes: PDFCrack is a GNU/Linux (other POSIX-compatible systems should work too) tool for recovering passwords and content from PDF-files.
It is small, command line driven without external dependencies.
